input:
In this worked example, we are going to calculate the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent heat exchanger in which a hot process stream is cooled from 160 °C all the way down to 120 °C, using cooling water that enters at 30 °C and leaves at 65 °C. The first thing to do is to work out the terminal temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger: at the hot end, the difference $\Delta T_1$ comes out at 95 K, while at the cold end the difference $\Delta T_2$ is 90 K. These two values are quite close to one another here. The log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is then given by the following well-known expression:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

Substituting the numbers into this expression gives a value of 92.5 K for $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is, as one might expect, fairly close to the simple arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences, since the two values happen to be quite close to each other in this particular case. It should be noted that this log-mean value rests on certain assumptions, namely that the overall heat transfer coefficient remains constant along the length of the exchanger and that no phase change takes place on either side, and if these assumptions do not hold then the result would need to be revisited accordingly.
target:
Calculate the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ for a countercurrent exchanger that cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 30 °C and leaving at 65 °C. The terminal differences are taken first. At the hot end, the process stream meets the leaving water and the difference $\Delta T_1$ is 95 K; at the cold end, the cooled stream meets the entering water and the difference $\Delta T_2$ is 90 K. A single mean difference is needed because the local difference varies along the exchanger while the duty calculation is written with one coefficient and one area. The log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is defined as the constant difference that transfers the same duty as the varying local difference, and for the two terminal differences it is

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

Substitution of the two terminal differences gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 92.5 K. The log-mean value lies between the two terminal differences and below their arithmetic mean, as it must: the logarithmic form weights the smaller difference more heavily, and a mean that ignored the variation along the exchanger would overstate the driving force at the cold end. The check on the result is its position: a value outside the interval bounded by the terminal differences would signal an error in the substitution. The value assumes a constant overall coefficient and no phase change on either side; a coefficient that varies along the exchanger, or a stream that condenses or boils, takes the calculation outside the relation, and the duty is then built up section by section with a local difference for each section instead.
